items.text: Swarm-manager's circuit_breaker.go (internal/execution/) implements a complete 3-state breaker: closed → open (at threshold) → half-open (after cooldown). Defaults: 3 consecutive failures to trip, 60-minute cooldown, auto-reset. File-backed with atomic JSON writes. This pattern can be adapted for vrooli-events by keying on {source}.{target}.{action} routes instead of item keys, and pushing state changes via SSE.

The graph broker (internal/graph/broker.go) provides the SSE design template: 30-second heartbeat via Ticker, 64-capacity buffered broadcast channel, non-blocking sends that drop if full, and stale client removal on write errors. For SSE, the heartbeat becomes a comment line (': heartbeat\n\n'), and Last-Event-ID enables reconnect-and-resume from the event store.

No retention or pruning logic exists anywhere in the codebase. Swarm-manager's eventlog accumulates events indefinitely and replays the full stream on startup. For vrooli-events (cross-scenario traffic at much higher volume), pruning is essential. A dual-trigger strategy (time window + size cap) with periodic background cleanup is the standard approach.

The discovery package hook point is callsite-level, not inside resolve.go itself. The resolver is a pure CLI wrapper — event emission should wrap the API client calls that USE the resolved URL, not the resolution itself. This means the emit-on-resolve hook lives in each scenario's discovery client initialization, not in the shared library.

items.context: The event store needs configurable retention to prevent unbounded growth. No pruning exists in the codebase today. Retention is dual-trigger: events are pruned when EITHER the time window OR the size cap is exceeded. A background goroutine runs the pruning query periodically. These defaults should be conservative (keep more, not less) since pruning is destructive.

options.label: 7-day window, 500MB size cap, prune every 1 hour
options.rationale: Aggressive pruning. Good for resource-constrained environments. Risk: may lose events needed for debugging recent issues.

options.label: 30-day window, 2GB size cap, prune every 6 hours
options.rationale: Balanced default. 30 days covers most debugging and audit needs. 2GB is modest for SQLite (WAL handles well). 6-hour prune cycle avoids unnecessary I/O.

options.label: 90-day window, 5GB size cap, prune every 24 hours
options.rationale: Conservative. Keeps a long history for compliance and deep investigation. Higher disk usage but SQLite handles multi-GB databases well with WAL.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify your own retention window, size cap, and prune interval

items.context: When multiple access control rules match an event (e.g., a broad 'deny all from scenario X' and a narrow 'allow scenario X for action Y'), the system needs a deterministic conflict resolution strategy. This affects how policy authors reason about rule interactions and how the cache evaluates rules.

options.label: Most-specific-wins: rules with more specific patterns (exact > prefix > glob) take precedence
options.rationale: Intuitive for policy authors — you can set broad defaults and add specific exceptions. Requires a specificity scoring algorithm. Used by CSS, firewall rules, and most policy engines.

options.label: Explicit-deny-wins: deny rules always override allow rules regardless of specificity
options.rationale: Simpler and more secure by default. If any rule says deny, it's denied. Easier to reason about but less flexible — you can't create exceptions to broad denials.

options.label: First-match: rules evaluated in priority order (lower number = higher priority), first match wins
options.rationale: Most flexible — full control over evaluation order. But requires policy authors to manage ordering, which is error-prone. Used by iptables.

items.topic: Proto envelope: typed payload vs opaque bytes
items.context: The settled envelope includes a `payload` field. The question is whether this should be opaque bytes (consumers deserialize based on event_type) or a proto `oneof` with typed payloads for known event categories. Agent-manager uses `oneof data` in RunEvent for discriminated unions. The choice affects schema evolution, code generation, and consumer ergonomics.

options.label: Opaque bytes: payload is bytes, consumers deserialize using event_type as discriminator
options.rationale: Maximum flexibility — new event types don't require envelope schema changes. Producers can emit any payload. Downside: no compile-time type safety for consumers, easy to send malformed payloads.

options.label: google.protobuf.Any: payload wraps a typed proto message with embedded type URL
options.rationale: Proto-native dynamic typing. Consumers can type-check at runtime using the type URL. Code generation provides helper methods. Slightly more overhead than raw bytes but much safer.

options.label: oneof with known types: payload is a oneof covering all known event payload types
options.rationale: Strongest type safety — compile-time exhaustive matching. But every new event type requires an envelope proto change, which defeats the extensibility of the metadata map approach.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own payload typing strategy
